Dear Sir/Madam, 
Sub: Notice of 38th Annual General Meeting (‘AGM’) and Integrated Annual Report 
for the financial year 2025-26  
We inform you that the 38th AGM of the Company is scheduled to be held on 
Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 9.00 A.M. IST through Video Conference/Other Audio-Visual Means. 
Pursuant to Regulation 34 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, please find enclosed the Notice convening the 38th AGM and the Integrated 
Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26, which are being sent through electronic mode to those 
Members whose e-mail addresses are registered with the Company/Registrar and Share Transfer 
Agent/Depositories. Further, a letter providing the web-link to access the AGM Notice and Integrated 
Annual Report is being sent to those Members who have not registered their e-mail address. 
The above documents can also be accessed on the website of the Company at: 
https://marico.com/india/investors/annual-report. 
This intimation is being made available on the website of the Company at: 
https://marico.com/india/investors/shareholder/stock-exchange.       
Kindly take the above on record. 
Thank you. 
Yours faithfully,

NOTICE is hereby given that the 38th Annual General Meeting of the Members of Marico Limited (“Company”) will be 
held on Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. IST through Video Conferencing/Other Audio-Visual Means to transact the 
following business: 
ORDINARY BUSINESS
1.	
To receive, consider and adopt the Audited Financial Statements (Standalone & Consolidated) of the Company for the financial 
year ended March 31, 2026, together with the reports of the Board of Directors and Statutory Auditors thereon.
2.	
To declare a Final Dividend of H 4 per equity share of H 1 each for the financial year ended March 31, 2026.
3.	
To appoint a Director in place of Mr. Rishabh Mariwala (DIN: 03072284), who retires by rotation and being eligible, offers 
himself for re-appointment.
SPECIAL BUSINESS
4.	
Ratify the remuneration payable to M/s. Ashwin Solanki & Associates, Cost Accountants (Firm 
Registration No. 100392), Cost Auditors of the Company for the financial year ending March 31, 2027
	
To consider and if thought fit, to pass with or without modification(s), the following resolution as an ORDINARY RESOLUTION:
	
“RESOLVED THAT pursuant to the provisions of Section 148 and other applicable provisions, if any, of the Companies Act, 
2013 and the relevant Rules made thereunder, as amended from time to time, the Members of the Company do hereby ratify the 
remuneration of H 11,00,000/- (Rupees Eleven Lakhs only), plus applicable taxes and reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses, 
if any, to M/s. Ashwin Solanki & Associates, Cost Accountants (Firm Registration No. 100392), as approved by the Board of 
Directors, for conducting audit of the cost records of the Company for the financial year ending March 31, 2027.”
Place: Mumbai
Date:  May 5, 2026

13.	INFORMATION ON FINAL DIVIDEND
	
a)	
The Board of Directors of the Company at its meeting 
held on May 5, 2026, recommended a final dividend 
of H 4 per equity share of H 1 each for the financial 
year 2025-26 (“Final Dividend”), subject to 
approval of the Members at the 38th AGM.
	
b)	
The Final Dividend, if approved by the Members, shall 
be paid on or before September 5, 2026 to the Members 
whose names appear in the Register of Members 
of the Company as on Thursday, July 30, 2026, 
being the record date fixed for this purpose. 
	
c)	
In accordance with Regulation 12 of the SEBI Listing 
Regulations dividend shall be paid only in electronic 
mode. In this regard, Members holding shares in 
physical/demat form are requested to ensure that their 
bank account details are updated with their respective 
Depository Participant/RTA, as the case may be, to enable 
the Company to make timely credit of dividend in their 
bank accounts. In case of physical folios wherein PAN 
and KYC details are not available, payment of dividend 
shall only be made electronically upon registering all the 
required details. For further information in this regard, 
please refer note no. 16 below.
	
d)	
Members are requested to note that as per the 
provisions of the Income Tax Act, 2025 (“IT Act”), 
dividends paid or distributed by a company shall be 
taxable in the hands of the Members. The Company 
shall therefore deduct tax at source (“TDS”) (at 
the applicable rates) at the time of payment of 
the Final Dividend. The withholding tax rate will 
vary depending on the residential status of the 
Member(s) and subject to verification of documents, 
uploaded by the Member(s) in this regard at 
https://web.in.mpms.mufg.com/formsreg/submission-
of-Form-121-41.html or submitted to the RTA at 
Investor.helpdesk@in.mpms.mufg.com. Members are 
requested to upload all documents at the 
aforesaid link only. 
	
e)	
The last date for Members to upload the requisite 
tax declarations on the above link is Thursday, 
July 30, 2026. The Company shall not 
consider any declarations received post 
the stipulated date.
	
f)	
A brief of the applicable TDS provisions under the 
IT Act for Resident and Non-resident Member(s) 
categories is given hereinbelow: 
	
	
(i)	
Resident Members: For Resident Members, 
TDS shall be deducted from the payment of 
Final Dividend if the dividend amount exceeds 
H 10,000/- in a financial year. In case of 
Resident Members whose PAN is registered with 
the depositories/RTA (as the case may be), TDS 
shall be deducted at source at the rate of 10% 
on the amount of dividend declared and paid 
by the Company during a financial year. If PAN 
is not registered/updated in the demat account/
folio as on the cut-off date or it is invalid or 
inoperative, TDS will be deducted at 20%. 
	
	
	
However, TDS shall not be deducted on the 
Final Dividend to resident individual Members 
where 
they 
provide 
Form 
121 
(earlier 
Form 15G/15H), subject to conditions specified 
in the IT Act. Further, in case of Resident Members 
having a Certificate issued under Section 395 of 
the IT Act, TDS will be deducted at the lower rate 
or no tax will be deducted, as specified therein, 
upon submission of such Certificate. PAN is 
mandatory for Members providing Form 121 or 
any other document as mentioned above.
	
	
	
Members should submit fresh declarations for 
the Final Dividend even if he/she has already 
submitted Form 121 to the Company earlier.
	
	
(ii)	
Non-resident Members: In the case of Non-
resident Members including Foreign Institutional 
Investors (FIIs)/Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), 
tax shall be deducted at 20% (plus applicable 
surcharge and cess) or Tax Treaty Rate (whichever 
is lower), subject to submission of self-attested 
copy of certificate of registration accorded 
under the relevant Regulations of SEBI. In order 
to avail the beneficial TDS rate as per respective 
Tax Treaty, following documents are required to 
be submitted by the Member to the RTA:
 
 
Copy of Indian Tax Identification Number 
(PAN), if available.
 
 
Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) obtained 
from the tax authorities of the country of 
which the Member is a resident, for the 
calendar year 2026.
 
 
Electronic Form 41 (earlier Form 10F) duly 
filled and signed.
 
 
Self-declaration 
from 
Non-resident 
individual/non-individual, in the format 
available on the Company’s website at 
https://marico.com/india/investors/
shareholder/dividend.
	
	
	
In case of Non-resident Members having an 
Certificate under Section 395 of the IT Act, TDS 
will be deducted at a lower rate or no tax will be 
deducted, as specified therein, upon submission 
of such Certificate.
Notice

g)	
Members are requested to note that earlier 
Form 15G/15H and Form 10F shall not be accepted 
for the purposes stated above.
	
h)	
In cases where Section 397 of the IT Act is applicable 
i.e. the Member has not submitted PAN/PAN is 
invalid/PAN is in-operative due to non-linking of 
PAN with Aadhaar, tax will be deducted at higher of 
the rates prescribed in Section 397 of the IT Act. The 
Company will be using functionality of the Income Tax 
Department for the above purpose 
	
	
The Company is not obligated to apply the beneficial Tax 
Treaty Rates at the time of tax deduction/withholding 
on dividend amounts. Application of beneficial Tax 
Treaty Rate shall depend upon the completeness of the 
documents submitted by Non-resident Members and 
review to the satisfaction of the Company.
	
i)	
Members who are exempted from TDS provisions 
through any circular or notification may need to 
provide documentary evidence in relation to the same 
to enable the Company in applying the appropriate 
TDS on Dividend payment to such Members. 
	
j)	
A General Communication on TDS on dividend 
informing the detailed procedure to be followed by 
Members, documents to be submitted and other details 
for availing the applicable tax rate will be sent to the 
Members in due course. The said communication 
will also be available on the Company’s website at 
https://marico.com/investorspdf/Communication-
of-TDS-on-Dividend.pdf.
14.	 ELECTRONIC DISPATCH OF ANNUAL REPORT 
AND PROCESS FOR REGISTRATION OF E-MAIL 
ADDRESS:
	
Pursuant to Sections 101 and 136 of the Act read with 
the relevant Rules made thereunder and Regulation 36 of 
the SEBI Listing Regulations, companies can send Annual 
Reports and other communications through electronic 
mode to those Members who have registered their e-mail 
address with the Company or Depositories. In accordance 
with the provisions of MCA Circulars and the SEBI Listing 
Regulations, Annual Report containing financial statements 
(including Report of Board of Directors, Auditor’s report 
or other documents required to be attached therewith), 
and such statements including Notice of the 38th AGM 
are being sent through electronic mode to those Members 
whose e-mail address is registered with the Company/RTA 
or the Depositories. 
	
Additionally, a letter providing the web-link to access 
Notice of the 38th AGM and Integrated Annual Report is 
being sent to those Members whose e-mail address is not 
registered with the Company/RTA or the Depositories. 
	
Members may note that Notice of the 38th AGM and 
the Annual Report 2025-26 are also available on the 
Company’s 
website 
at 
https://marico.com/india/
investors/documentation/annual-reports, website of the

National Stock Exchange of India Limited: www.nseindia.com. 
Notice of the 38th AGM is also disseminated on the website 
of CDSL i.e. www.evotingindia.com.

are requested to make service requests in prescribed

17.	 SEBI has mandated the submission of PAN by every 
participant in the securities market. Members holding 
shares in dematerialised form are therefore requested to 
submit their PAN to the Depository Participant(s) with whom 
they maintain their dematerialised accounts. 
18.	 Pursuant to the provisions of Section 72 of the Act read with 
the Rules made thereunder, Members holding shares in a 
single name may avail the facility of nomination in respect 
of the shares held by them. All holders of physical securities 
are encouraged in their own interest to provide choice 
of nomination. The Company has sent communications 
to the concerned shareholders explaining the aforesaid 
requirements and the same can also be accessed at: 
https://marico.com/india/investors/shareholder/standard-norms. 
Members may avail this facility by sending a nomination 
in the prescribed Form No. SH-13 to the RTA. The said 
form is available on the Company’s website and can be 
downloaded using the aforesaid weblink. 
	
Further, if shares are held in Dematerialised form, Members 
can contact their respective Depository Participant(s) to 
update their nomination details.
19.	 Members may note that, as mandated by SEBI, effective 
April 1, 2019, the Company cannot process any request 
for transfer of securities in physical mode. Only securities 
held in Dematerialised form can be transferred. Hence, 
Members are requested to Dematerialise their shares if held 
in physical form.
	
Pursuant to SEBI Circular No. HO/38/13/11(2)2026-
MIRSD-POD/I/3750/2026 dated January 30, 2026, 
a Special Window has been opened for transfer and 
dematerialization of physical shares sold or purchased prior to 
April 1, 2019 including for the transfer request(s) which were 
rejected/returned/not attended due to deficiency in documents/
process or otherwise. This Special Window shall remain 
open for a period of 1 (one) year from February 5, 2026 to 
February 4, 2027. Further details in this regard are 
available on the website of the Company at https://marico.
com/india/investors/shareholder/special-window. 
20.	 Members who wish to claim dividends that remain 
unclaimed/unpaid are requested to submit their request to 
the RTA (at details mentioned hereinbelow) or the Company 
Secretary at the Company’s Registered Office or e-mail 
at investor@marico.com. Members are requested to note 
that dividends that are not claimed or remain unpaid for 
7 (seven) years from the date of transfer to the Company’s 
unpaid dividend account will be/are transferred to the 
Investor Education and Protection Fund (“IEPF”). Further, 
equity shares in respect whereof dividend remains 
unclaimed/unpaid for 7 (seven) consecutive years will also 
be transferred to the IEPF as per Section 124 of the Act read 
with Rules notified thereunder, as may be amended from 
time to time. The Members whose unclaimed dividends/
shares have been transferred to IEPF may claim the same 
by making an online application to the IEPF Authority 
in web Form IEPF-5. The said form can be accessed at 
http://www.iepf.gov.in/.
21.	 Pursuant to the Rule 5(8) of the Investor Education and 
Protection Authority (Accounting, Audit, Transfer and 
Refund) Rules, 2016, the Company has uploaded details 
of unpaid and unclaimed amounts lying with the Company 
on its website at https://marico.com/india/investors/
documentation/dividend. 
22.	 As per circulars issued by SEBI from time to time, investors 
have been provided with an option for dispute resolution 
under the Stock Exchange arbitration mechanism where 
they can opt for arbitration with Stock Exchanges in case of 
any grievance with the Company and/or RTA.
	
Further, investors can also register their complaint on the 
Online Dispute Resolution Portal, a mechanism for online 
resolution of disputes arising in the Indian Securities 
Market. Further details in this regard are available on 
the Company’s website at https://marico.com/india/
investors/shareholder/share-holders-guide.
23.	 Any person becoming a Member of the Company after the 
Notice of the AGM is sent out through e-mail and holds 
shares as on the cut-off date i.e. Thursday, July 30, 2026, 
may obtain the user ID and password by sending a request 
to helpdesk.evoting@cdslindia.com and can exercise their

24.	 Pursuant to Section 108 and other applicable provisions, if 
any, of the Act read with the Companies (Management and 
Administration) Rules, 2014, as amended, Regulation 44 
of the SEBI Listing Regulations and the MCA Circulars, 
facility for Remote e-voting and e-voting during the meeting 
is provided to the Members in respect of the resolutions 
proposed in this Notice using the platform of CDSL.
25.	 In order to increase the efficiency of voting process and in terms 
of SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD/CIR/P/2020/242 
dated December 9, 2020, Demat account holders are being 
provided a single login credential, through their demat 
accounts/websites of Depositories/Depository Participants.

without having to register again with the e-voting service 
providers, thereby facilitating seamless authentication, 
enhancing ease and convenience of participating in the

26.	 A facility for e-voting at the AGM will be made available 
to the Members who have not already cast their votes by 
Remote e-voting prior to the Meeting. Members who have 
cast their votes by Remote e-voting prior to the Meeting may 
participate in the AGM but shall not be entitled to cast their 
votes during the Meeting.
27.	 Voting rights shall be reckoned on the paid-up value of 
equity shares registered in the name of the Members as 
on the cut-off date i.e. Thursday, July 30, 2026. A 
person, whose name is recorded in the Register of Members 
or in the Register of Beneficial Owners (in case of electronic 
shareholding) maintained by the Depositories as on the 
cut-off date, i.e. Thursday, July 30, 2026 only shall be 
entitled to avail the facility of Remote e-voting and e-voting 
at the AGM. A person who is not a Member as on the cut-off 
date should treat this Notice for information purposes only.
28.	 The Remote e-voting period commences from 9:00 a.m. IST 
on Monday, August 3, 2026 and ends at 5:00 p.m. IST 
on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. The Remote e-voting 
module shall be disabled by CDSL thereafter. Once the vote 
on a resolution is cast by the Member, the Member shall not 
be allowed to change it subsequently.

able to access the system of all e-voting service providers.

Pursuant to the provisions of Section 152 and other applicable 
provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act”) and the

third of these Directors must retire from office at each Annual 
General Meeting (“AGM”), but each retiring director is eligible for 
re-election at such meeting. Currently, Independent Directors and 
the Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer are not subject 
to retirement by rotation. Accordingly, Mr. Rishabh Mariwala 
(DIN: 03072284) retires by rotation at the 38th AGM and being 
eligible, has offered himself for re-appointment.
Mr. Rishabh Mariwala is a seasoned investor and a second-
generation business entrepreneur. He has a hands-on 
entrepreneurial experience across all aspects of the business 
and has worked across several roles including projects, service 
quality management and online marketing. Keeping in view his 
deep consumer insights in FMCG industry, especially the start-up 
space, and diverse experience and contribution to the Company’s 
long-term strategic imperatives, the Board of Directors (“Board”) 
is of the opinion that it will be in the interest of the Company to 
re-appoint him as a Non-Executive Director. 
With regard to the proposed re-appointment as aforesaid, the 
Company has received from Mr. Rishabh Mariwala consent to act 
as Director in terms of Section 152 of the Act, declaration that he 
is not disqualified from being appointed as Director in terms of 
Section 164 of the Act, and other requisite consents, declarations 
and disclosures as applicable. 
Additional information in respect of Mr. Rishabh Mariwala, 
pursuant to Regulation 36 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and the Secretarial 
Standard on General Meetings (SS-2), is given at Annexure A 
and his brief profile is provided at Annexure B to this Notice.

MESSAGE FROM THE CHAIRMAN
Empowered by Purpose-led Growth 
in a Decade of Transformation
In the year under review, your Company’s performance across 
key parameters was encouraging and reaffirmed Marico’s 
resilience and clarity of purpose. Despite a complex global 
environment marked by input cost volatility and geopolitical 
developments, Marico demonstrated agility and consistency, 
while remaining focused on long‑term growth, portfolio 
transformation, and digital enablement. The Company 
continued to strengthen its core franchises, expand into adjacent 
categories, and build capabilities that enhance the quality and 
sustainability of growth.
As we look to the future, our strategic vision remains anchored 
in delivering sustainable and profitable growth by staying 
attuned to evolving consumer needs and operating with agility in 
a dynamic environment. The building blocks of our strategy -  
category leadership, premiumisation, market expansion, 
and digital enablement, continue to guide our priorities and 
investments, supported by execution with rigor. We continue to 
leverage our three core assets, our brands, our talent and our 
culture, as key enablers of long‑term value creation. Together, 
these strengths position us to unlock the next horizon of growth 
while remaining true to our purpose.
FY26 marked an important milestone in Marico’s growth journey, 
with the Company delivering multi‑year high consolidated revenue 
growth, volume growth in the India business and constant‑currency 
growth in international markets. This performance reflects the 
enduring strength of our brands, the effectiveness of our portfolio 
choices, and the commitment of our people, as well as the 
continued trust of our stakeholders. As we build on this momentum, 
we remain sharply focused on our Vision 2030 aspirations, 
guided by a clear roadmap rooted in innovation, purposeful brand 
building, and operational excellence.
Innovation & Digital Transformation: Building for 
the Future
Innovation remains integral to Marico’s growth journey. During 
FY26, we continued to invest thoughtfully in strengthening 
our innovation pipeline and focused on addressing changing 
consumer needs for better efficacy, convenience and 
holistic wellness. Simultaneously, we accelerated our digital 
transformation agenda. Data analytics, AI-led insights, and 
enhanced consumer engagement platforms are increasingly 
reshaping how we build brands, deepen personalisation and 
improve speed-to-market. These capabilities are enabling 
sharper decision-making across marketing, supply chain and 
demand forecasting.
The Marico Innovation Foundation (MIF) continues to serve as a 
key catalyst in strengthening the innovation ecosystem beyond 
our balance sheet. Through its flagship Scale‑Up programme, 
MIF supports high‑potential ventures across the circular 
economy, agri‑tech, and climate solutions, reinforcing our 
belief that innovation can deliver meaningful impact at scale. 
During the year, the programme onboarded new innovations 
and continued to support a cohort of high‑potential Indian 
startups through mentorship that extends well beyond capital. 
The agri‑pilot programme progressed to an advanced phase, 
with emphasis on farmer awareness and capability building. 
A comprehensive baseline survey covering 1,000 farmers 
across Mirzapur and Varanasi provided valuable insights into 
on‑ground realities, while preparatory work for technology 
deployment is underway.
Sustainability & ESG: Progress with Purpose
FY26 marked meaningful progress against our ESG 2030 
Roadmap, anchored in climate action, circularity, responsible 
sourcing, people well-being, and robust governance. Our 
continued commitment to sustainability and responsible business 
practices is reflected in the strong external recognition we have 
received across leading global benchmarks. During the year, 
we made significant progress across our key ESG focus areas, 
strengthening our commitment to sustainable and responsible 
growth. In climate action, we achieved an 89.3% reduction in 
operational GHG emissions intensity (Scope 1 and 2 emissions) 
against our FY13 baseline, with renewable energy now 
accounting for 77.3% of our total consumption. I am also proud 
to share that two of our manufacturing units, Perundurai and 
Jalgaon, have achieved carbon neutrality.

Water stewardship continues to remain a cornerstone of our 
sustainability agenda. We have achieved 100% operational 
water footprint offset through robust water conservation 
potential creation initiatives, cumulatively generating over 547 
crore litres. In addition, we have ensured 100% recycling and 
reuse of effluents, with two of our manufacturing units now 
Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD)-certified. Our progress towards 
a circular economy is evident in our packaging initiatives, 
with 95% of our packaging now recyclable. Additionally, 
two of our manufacturing units have achieved Zero Waste to 
Landfill certification. In responsible sourcing, we continue to 
deepen engagement with our partners, with 88% of our critical 
business associates certified at Level 1 and 43% at Level 2, 
reinforcing our commitment to ethical and sustainable supply 
chains. Around 92% of our sourcing (by spends) is derived from 
indigenous sources. As plastic waste continues to rise, the need 
for scalable recycling solutions and resilient circular systems has 
become increasingly critical. Our efforts span the value chain – 
from advancing recyclable packaging solutions to strengthening 
recovery infrastructure and actively contributing to collaborative 
platforms such as the India Plastics Pact.
Lastly, our strong governance framework remains the foundation 
of our sustainability journey, with 100% employee certification 
on our Code of Conduct and 86% of our business associates 
aligned to our ethical standards. Together, these milestones 
reflect our belief that sustainability is not a destination, 
but a continuous journey of improvement, innovation, and 
accountability.
Community & Social Impact: Creating Enduring 
Value
Beyond business, Marico remains deeply committed to creating 
positive societal impact at scale. Our flagship initiatives in 
farmer empowerment, education, nutrition, skill development, 
and public health continued to expand their reach during the 
year. Thousands of farmers have benefited from improved 
agricultural practices through our interventions, while education 
and livelihood initiatives enabled opportunities for women, 
children and underserved communities.
Our brands remain purpose-driven at their core. Through our 
PKF (Parachute Kalpavriksha Foundation) programme, we 
are advancing sustainable agriculture, supporting over 2.05 
lakh farmers, with 4.97 lakh acres of farmland under our 
programmes. Through this programme, farmers are empowered 
with best scientific farming practices in areas such as soil health, 
water management, and pest control under expert guidance. 
This has resulted in a ~15%+ improvement in differential 
productivity. Nihar Naturals, on the other hand, continues to 
drive social impact by supporting education for underprivileged 
children, benefiting over 2.12 lakh students and 0.63 lakh 
teachers in FY26. The Nihar Shanti Pathshala Funwala initiative 
continues to promote education and livelihood opportunities, 
particularly for women, children, elderly, differently-abled, 
and underserved communities. Our approach integrates brand 
purpose with societal needs, enabling us to create lasting and 
meaningful impact across communities.
Driven by a deep sense of purpose, Marico continues to harness 
the reputation and recall of its brands to enhance meaningful 
societal impact. Your Company’s sustainability efforts extend 
beyond decarbonisation and water stewardship programmes 
to include sustainable agriculture, livelihood enhancement and 
brand-led social transformation.
People & Culture: The Marico Way
At the heart of Marico’s success lies its people and culture. 
Our values of agility, ownership, resilience, and openness 
continued to guide us through a dynamic year. We remain 
committed to offering each Mariconian the opportunity to create 
winning brands and work in an inspiring environment to drive 
innovation, growth and sustainable business. Our focus is to 
provide the diverse talent at Marico with an inclusive culture of 
Equality, Belongingness and Openness. We believe that a strong 
culture is not just an enabler of performance, it is the foundation 
of long-term value creation.
The culture at Marico is one of agility and openness, along 
with the willingness and humility to learn and transform with 
changing times. Investments in talent development, leadership 
capability building, and diversity initiatives have further 
strengthened our organisational fabric.
At Marico, every product begins with a purpose. We go beyond 
developing formulations and packaging – we create meaningful 
consumer experiences rooted in science, sustainability, and 
well-being.
Governance & Leadership: Trust as a Pillar
Strong governance remains central to Marico’s operating 
philosophy. I would like to acknowledge the Board’s continued 
guidance in shaping strategy, strengthening risk management 
and upholding the highest standards of transparency and 
accountability. I am also pleased to welcome Mr. Bhaskar Bhat 
and Mr. Girish Paranjpe as Independent Directors on the Board. 
Both bring with them deep experience, sound judgement, and 
diverse perspectives, which I am confident will further strengthen 
the Board’s deliberations and add meaningful value to the 
Company’s long‑term journey.
In an increasingly complex environment shaped by climate 
change, geopolitical developments, and economic uncertainties, 
resilience and agility are critical. Over the years, we have built 
robust systems and processes that are continuously refined to 
ensure Marico remains future-ready and resilient.
Future Outlook: Navigating with Confidence
Building a business is not only about scale – it is about clarity 
of purpose, the courage to evolve, and the discipline to stay the 
course with resilience and responsibility. As we look ahead to 
FY27, we remain focused on strengthening our growth engines, 
deepening innovation capabilities, and accelerating our 
sustainability agenda. While macroeconomic and geopolitical 
uncertainties persist, we enter the new year with confidence, 
supported by a resilient business model, strong brands, and an 
agile organisation. Our long-term vision remains unchanged: 
to deliver profitable growth, create enduring stakeholder 
value, and make a meaningful difference to society. Over 
three decades ago, Marico began its journey with a simple 
yet powerful aspiration – to build a company that makes a 
difference. What began as a modest start has evolved into 
a purpose-driven organisation, guided by strong values and 
a distinctive culture. As we step into the next decade, this 
purpose continues to shape every decision we make. Marico 
is now building the next decade's growth engines: digital-first, 
premium, and globally scalable brands in multiple markets 
without compromising Marico’s DNA of disciplined value 
creation.
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to our Board 
members for their invaluable guidance, our employees for their 
unwavering commitment, and our customers, partners, suppliers, 
and investors for their continued trust and support. Above all, I 
thank the communities we serve for believing in our philosophy 
of ‘Making a Difference’.
Together, we will continue to shape Marico’s next chapter with 
confidence, responsibility, and purpose.

MESSAGE FROM THE MD AND CEO
I am pleased to share my reflections with you as we present Marico’s 
Integrated Annual Report for the year ended March 31, 2026.
FY26 marked a year of strong execution in a challenging 
operating environment. Despite elevated input costs, geopolitical 
developments, and evolving consumption trends across markets, 
your Company delivered top-quartile performance across key 
parameters. Volume growth in the India business, constant 
currency growth in the international markets, and consolidated 
revenue growth reached multi-year highs, underscoring the 
strength of our brands, strategic clarity and rigor in execution. 
Importantly, we complemented our robust performance, with 
consistent and meaningful progress on our strategic priorities. 
Marico is steadily evolving into a well-diversified, multi-national 
FMCG company, with a growing presence in Premium Personal 
Care, Foods, Digital-First and International businesses. This 
transformation is deliberate and measured, anchored in building 
scalable and profitable businesses in large categories with long 
runway for growth.
As we look ahead, our focus remains clear: strengthen our core 
franchises, expand into adjacencies where we have a right to win, 
scale up our digital businesses profitably and further diversify our 
international growth engine. This balanced approach enables 
us to deliver consistent growth while enhancing the quality and 
resilience of our portfolio.
Encouragingly, as we progress towards our aspiration of H15,000 
crore in revenues, we have already reached H13,611 crore, 
reinforcing our confidence in sustaining the growth momentum. 
Building on this foundation, under Vision 2030, we aim to 
achieve H20,000 crores in revenues, delivering sustained double-
digit revenue growth alongside mid-teens EBITDA growth.
FY26 - Strong and Resilient Performance Amidst 
Volatile Operating Environment.
The operating environment during the year was shaped by 
a complex interplay of macroeconomic factors and evolving 
consumption trends across markets. On one side, elevated input 
costs resulted in pricing actions in select categories, influencing 
consumption behaviour and affordability. At the same time, 
demand patterns continued to shift, with consumers increasingly 
gravitating towards premium propositions. Favourable policy 
measures including GST rate rationalisation during the year has 
benefited consumption at large and improved consumer sentiments. 
India Business: Core Strengthens Along With

Reimagining Sustainable Value 
Creation for a Transformative Decade
At Marico, materiality is not viewed merely as a reporting requirement; 
it is a strategic compass that shapes how we anticipate change, 
strengthen resilience, create long-term value and remain relevant in an 
increasingly complex and rapidly evolving world.
As global business systems undergo 
profound transformation driven 
by climate volatility, technological 
disruption, geopolitical uncertainty, 
resource constraints and evolving societal 
expectations, sustainability considerations 
are becoming deeply intertwined with 
enterprise value creation. Increasingly, 
the organisations that will lead the future 
are those capable of balancing growth 
with responsibility, agility with resilience, 
and innovation with measurable impact.
At Marico, we recognise that the coming 
decade will fundamentally redefine 
how businesses operate, compete and 
create value. Our materiality assessment 
therefore extends beyond identifying 
present-day priorities; it enables 
us to evaluate emerging ESG risks, 
opportunities and systemic megatrends 
expected to shape the future of the 
FMCG sector and influence long-term 
business sustainability.
Our materiality approach is deeply 
integrated with our ESG 2030 roadmap 
and serves as a foundational pillar for 
strategic decision-making, enterprise 
risk management, governance oversight 
and stakeholder engagement. It enables 
us to focus our efforts on the issues that 
matter most — not only to our business 
and investors, but also to society, the 
environment and future generations.
Aligned with evolving global frameworks 
and investor expectations, our assessment 
incorporates the concept of double 
materiality by evaluating both:
	 The impact of ESG issues on Marico’s 
business performance, resilience and 
long-term value creation; and 
	 Marico’s impact on the economy, 
environment and society through its 
operations, products and value chain. 
Through this lens, sustainability becomes 
not a parallel agenda, but a core 
business imperative shaping the future 
trajectory of Marico.
Materiality in an Era of Global 
Transition
The sustainability landscape is evolving 
at an unprecedented pace. Issues once 
considered peripheral are now central 
to investor confidence, operational 
continuity, regulatory preparedness and 
brand trust.
Climate change, biodiversity loss, supply 
chain disruptions, water insecurity, 
circular economy transitions and social 
inequalities are fundamentally reshaping 
expectations from businesses globally. 
Simultaneously, capital markets are 
increasingly integrating ESG performance 
into investment and stewardship decisions, 
with heightened focus on:
	 Climate resilience and transition 
preparedness 
	 Scope 3 emissions and 
decarbonisation pathways 
	 Nature and biodiversity stewardship 
	 Human rights due diligence 
	 Ethical and traceable supply chains 
	 Circular packaging systems 
	 Sustainable product innovation 
	 Governance transparency and 
accountability 
In this evolving landscape, materiality 
enables Marico to proactively identify 
strategic priorities, anticipate emerging 
risks and strengthen long-term resilience 
in a rapidly changing world.

anniversary of World Environment Day, we transitioned to the ESG 2030 Roadmap.

through eight thematic focus areas:

and 50% certification of Level 2 critical 
suppliers.

minimize waste across the value chain.

Make a difference to our stakeholders by 
driving five purposeful brand programs.
Sustainable Agriculture:
Boost economic self-sufficiency of farmers 
by improving the productivity of their 
farms.
Inclusion and Diversity:
Create an inclusive and diverse culture 
and work environment.
Corporate Governance:
Ensuring corporate governance by 
practicing ethical business practices and 
robust risk mitigation.
Innovation:
Developing sustainable 
product portfolios that meet 
evolving consumer aspirations.
Risk Governance:
Strengthening our social 
license to operate through 
transparency and impact 
measurement.
Water Stewardship:
Replenish more water annually than is 
consumed in manufacturing operations.
Operational Excellence: 
Implementing resource-
efficient manufacturing 
processes.
Climate Action:
Achieve Net Zero emissions across India 
operations by 2040.
Strategic Planning:
Aligning long-term growth 
with planetary boundaries.

rather than a parallel agenda. By aligning our priorities with emerging global ESG 
ratings and frameworks, we anticipate regulatory shifts and de-risk our value chains. 
The roadmap serves as a catalyst for capital allocation and the design of resilient 
manufacturing systems. It transforms sustainability into a driver for innovation and 
competitive advantage, ensuring Marico leads with accountability in a climate-
conscious market.
By embedding these priorities, we ensure 
that every action taken today contributes 
to a transformative, future-ready business 
model that creates enduring value for all

sustaining growth, and creating long-term 
value for stakeholders.

independent assurance on the effectiveness

business strategy and operational objectives.

Management Committee, provides robust 
oversight, while risk ownership is embedded

assessments, scenario planning and stress testing

response strategies.

Partnering with Purpose for

Stakeholder engagement forms a critical pillar of our sustainability journey and 
responsible business conduct. At Marico, we adopt an inclusive, transparent, 
and agile approach to engagement, enabling us to create enduring value while 
effectively addressing the expectations of stakeholders who influence or are impacted 
by our operations. This approach is guided by our commitment to stakeholder 
capitalism, which shapes how we create shared value across our ecosystem. At its 
core, this philosophy is anchored in four interconnected principles:
Principle of Governance
Advancing environmental responsibility 
through efficient resource use and climate-
conscious actions.
Upholding accountability, integrity, 
and stewardship across all 
decision-making processes.
Planet
Promoting a culture 
rooted in dignity, equality, 
diversity, and inclusion.
People
Creating sustainable value by aligning with the 
evolving needs and aspirations of our stakeholders.
Prosperity
Marico’s Stakeholder Engagement 
framework plays a critical role in shaping 
its sustainability strategy and governance 
approach by enabling continuous dialogue 
with investors, consumers, employees, 
value-chain partners, communities, 
regulators, and industry bodies. Insights 
gathered through these engagements 
inform the Company’s Double Materiality 
Assessment (DMA), helping identify and 
prioritise ESG topics that are material 
both from a financial impact perspective 
and from the standpoint of Marico’s 
impact on society and the environment. 
The outcomes of this process are further 
integrated into enterprise risk management 
systems, ESG target setting under the 
ESG 2030 Roadmap, policy evolution, 
and sustainability disclosures across 
reporting platforms. This stakeholder-
centric approach enables Marico to 
proactively address emerging ESG risks 
and opportunities, strengthen governance 
mechanisms, and enhance transparency 
and accountability in disclosures aligned 
with global and national frameworks. This 
integrated approach reflects alignment 
with Global Reporting Initiative 
GRI 2-29 on stakeholder 
engagement, SEBI BRSR Principle 
4 on responsiveness towards 
stakeholder interests, and the 
United Nations Guiding Principles 
on Business and Human Rights, 
reinforcing Marico’s commitment to 
inclusive, transparent, and responsible 
business conduct.
Approach to Stakeholder 
Engagement
At Marico, stakeholder engagement is 
embedded as a strategic lever for driving 
sustainable and inclusive value creation. 
Our approach is anchored in a structured 
and insight-led framework that enables us 
to systematically identify, prioritise, and 
engage with stakeholders across the value 
chain. Stakeholder groups are identified 
through a comprehensive assessment 
of their alignment with our purpose, 
as well as their relevance, influence, 
and proximity to our operations. Based 
on this evaluation, stakeholders are 
mapped and prioritised according to 
their level of impact on, and interest in, 
our business. This ensures a focused and 
meaningful engagement approach. We 
deploy tailored engagement mechanisms 
for each stakeholder group, enabling 
consistent, transparent, and context-
specific interactions. Insights gathered 
through these engagements are actively 
integrated into our decision-making 
processes shaping our sustainability 
priorities and guiding ESG interventions 
in line with stakeholder expectations 
and our long-term strategy. The process 
incorporates dynamic materiality 
considerations, enabling the Company to 
continuously evaluate evolving impacts, 
dependencies, risks, and opportunities 
across the value chain assessed from 
both financial materiality and impact 
materiality perspectives in line with 
emerging global disclosure standards. 
The rigour of the assessment is further 
strengthened through structured cross-
functional participation involving teams 
across sustainability, risk management, 
procurement, legal and compliance, 
human resources, operations, investor 
relations, and business functions. This 
enterprise-wide integration ensures that 
stakeholder insights inform strategic 
decisions in a cohesive and holistic 
manner, rather than in functional silos. In 
addition, Marico incorporates external 
benchmarking inputs to ensure alignment 
with evolving global standards and 
investor expectations.
Criteria and Methodology for 
Stakeholder Identification
Our stakeholder identification process 
is guided by the principles of inclusivity, 
materiality, and responsiveness. 
Stakeholders are assessed based on their 
potential to influence, or be influenced 
by, our business activities, sustainability 
performance, and value creation journey. 
This assessment is supported by a 
structured methodology that evaluates 
stakeholders across key dimensions 
such as influence, dependence, strategic 
importance, and regulatory interface. 
The outcome is a prioritised set of 
stakeholder groups, including consumers, 
investors and shareholders, employees 
(including contractual workforce), 
value chain partners, government and 
regulatory bodies, and communities. 
These insights form the foundation of 
our stakeholder engagement strategy 
and inform our sustainability disclosures, 
ensuring alignment with evolving 
stakeholder expectations and global ESG 
frameworks.
Stakeholders are identified and 
assessed based on two core 
dimensions: their influence on 
Marico’s business decisions 
and operations, and their 
dependency on or exposure 
to the Company’s activities 
and impacts. This assessment 
forms the basis of a Stakeholder 
Prioritisation Matrix that determines 
the depth, frequency, and mode of 
engagement for each stakeholder 
category through channels such as 
investor interactions, employee forums, 
supplier assessments, consumer 
feedback mechanisms, community 
consultations, regulatory dialogues, 
independent audits, and grievance 
redressal platforms. The insights 
emerging from these engagements are 
systematically integrated into Marico’s 
Double Materiality Assessment, wherein 
sustainability topics are evaluated from 
both financial materiality and impact 
materiality perspectives. Topics identified 
through stakeholder consultations 
are assessed based on stakeholder 
significance, business relevance, risk 
exposure, and strategic importance, 
resulting in a consolidated Materiality 
Matrix that defines Marico’s priority ESG 
themes. The outcomes of this process 
served as critical inputs in shaping 
Marico’s ESG Framework and its 2030 
roadmap, including the prioritization of 
strategic focus areas.
For more details on Marico's Materiality 
assessment, please refer to the 
"Sustainability at Marico" chapter in this 
Report

From Struggles to 
Sustainability:  
A Farmer’s Journey of 
Transformation
In Kulichettipalayam near Pollachi, Coimbatore, farmer Mr. 
Ravichandran manages a 10 acre coconut farm with over 600 
trees. Like many smallholders, he faced persistent challenges 
- tree diseases, root infestations, and rising input costs that 
strained both productivity and profitability.
His turning point came when the Parachute Kalpavriksha 
Foundation (PKF) team, led by Mr. Aravind, visited his farm 
and conducted a detailed assessment. They identified critical 
issues and provided practical, science based recommendations: 
introducing sunn hemp as a cover crop, applying urea and 
neem cake, painting trunks with calcium hydroxide, and using 
root feeding treatments to control whitefly infestations.
The results were remarkable. Before adopting PKF’s guidance, 
the farm yielded around 600 coconuts. After implementation, 
harvests rose dramatically to 8-8.5 loads of coconuts, while 
soil testing and tailored inputs improved soil health. Input costs 
reduced substantially, and profitability increased - proving that 
sustainable practices can drive both productivity and resilience.
Beyond technical solutions, PKF’s continuous support made 
a lasting difference. Mr. Ravichandran received regular field 
visits, phone guidance, and advice on irrigation practices. 
With their encouragement, he developed a small farm pond to 
manage water resources more effectively, ensuring long term 
sustainability.
Today, his farm stands as a model of transformation - 
showcasing how knowledge, innovation, and dedicated 
support can empower farmers to overcome challenges and 
thrive. Mr. Ravichandran’s journey reflects the true impact 
of PKF’s mission: strengthening livelihoods, improving 
productivity, and building sustainable farming communities.

Resilient Farming: 
Palanisamy’s Transformation
Mr. Palanisamy, a 65 year old coconut farmer from 
Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu, exemplifies how integrated 
agricultural support can transform livelihoods. Cultivating six 
acres of coconut, his farm was once plagued by severe pest 
infestations, declining yields, poor nut weight, and recurring 
water scarcity. White fly attacks forced him to cut down nearly 
20% of trees annually, while unreliable irrigation further 
constrained productivity.
The turning point came when he engaged with the 
Kalpavriksha initiative under Marico’s Sustainable Agriculture 
program. Supported by a field service provider (FSP), he 
gradually adopted improved practices such as mulching, 
bush cutting, root feeding, drip irrigation, and better fertiliser 
application. Regular field visits and technical handholding 
strengthened pest surveillance and nutrient management, while 
farmer meetings connected him to government schemes and 
modern techniques.
Parallel support from the Jalashay project addressed his most 
pressing challenge-water scarcity. Construction of a farm pond 
enabled rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge, 
ensuring more reliable irrigation across seasons.
Within a year, Palanisamy observed significant improvements. 
Pest incidence dropped, tree vitality improved, and coconut 
yield and nut quality rose. His income from coconut cultivation 
increased by nearly 30%, bringing greater financial stability to 
his household. Enhanced soil moisture retention and consistent 
irrigation further sustained productivity gains.
Digital engagement through the Kalpavriksha mobile app 
and advisory helpline kept him updated on market prices, 
fertiliser norms, and government schemes in his local language, 
strengthening his confidence in independent farm management.
Palanisamy’s journey demonstrates how combining scientific 
farm practices, water infrastructure, and continuous extension 
support can help smallholder farmers overcome constraints, 
achieve resilience, and unlock sustainable growth.

create lasting impact on communities and ecosystems.
Focused on addressing post monsoon water scarcity 
and reducing reliance on groundwater, the program 
builds community water storage solutions through 
effective recharge measures. Detailed water assessments 
and participatory water budgeting are carried out in 
each project area, enabling targeted interventions and 
measurable progress toward water security.
Currently active across Maharashtra (Jalgaon), Tamil 
Nadu (Coimbatore, Pollachi, Theni), Gujarat (Sanand, 
Junagadh), and Pondicherry, Jalashay promotes 
efficient water demand management to support multi 
crop cultivation and strengthen agricultural resilience. 
Its participatory model engages local communities, 
government bodies, and NGOs in water governance 
while raising awareness on sustainable practices 
such as drip irrigation, climate resilient agriculture, 
vermicomposting, afforestation, and water budgeting.
Anchored in a dual framework-Paanishala (demand 
side interventions) and Jal Samruddhi (supply side 
interventions)-the initiative ensures both conservation and 
augmentation of water resources. 
Aligned with the Sustainable Development 
Goals, notably SDG 6 (Clean Water and 
Sanitation) Jalashay creates integrated value for 
communities and ecosystems, ensuring resilience 
and sustainability for the future.

Programme: Water

Jitendra and his wife Shital live in Devhari village in Jalgaon 
district of North Maharashtra. For many years, their main 
challenge was the lack of water on their 7 acre farm. Their dug 
well, 50 feet deep and the small naala beside the land were 
the only sources of water. Every year, Jitendra felt restricted in 
choosing crops because the water never lasted long enough.
Three years ago, Jitendra grew cotton on all 7 acres during 
Kharif. In the Rabi season, due to limited water, he could 
cultivate wheat and harbhara on only 2.5 acres, as his 
well used to dry up by December and the naala by March. 
Constructing a farm pond was not possible for him due to the 
financial constraints and land requirement.
In 2023, a meeting was called in the village under the Marico’s 
Jalashay Jalsamruddhi Project. The idea was naala deepening. 
When Jitendra heard that a bit of land from each farmer would 
be needed, his family became worried. Giving up land, even 
a small portion, was not an easy decision. After discussing the 
long-term benefits, they agreed. Other farmers also supported 
the activity, and the work was taken up collectively.
The well, which dried by December earlier, now had water till 
the end of February. The naala stayed filled till May. With this 
confidence, Jitendra changed his cropping pattern. He started 
cultivating dadar (2.5 acres), jowar (2.5 acres), wheat (2 
acres), and brinjal (0.5 acre). From the second crop, he earns 
around H70,000, which was not possible earlier.
His dependence on loans has reduced by almost 60% because 
of improved yields and lower expenses. He now grows his own 
fodder, which has further decreased costs. With assured water 
and fodder, he increased the number of livestock and supplies 
milk to the dairy, adding a steady income source.

In Asalgam village of Viramgam block, South Gujarat, farming

season farming. They began cultivating castor in the kharif 
season and sesame in the summer. That summer crop alone 
added nearly H1.2 lakh to their annual income-more than 
doubling what they once earned.

dignity and confidence. Their land, once idle, now thrived year 
round. Their family’s needs were met with stability, and their 
pride in farming returned.

acres to 12 acres, introducing sweet lemon alongside custard 
apples, while continuing his organic practices.

migration of laborers for sugarcane harvesting. For Dattatray, the 
intervention brought more than higher yields - it restored confidence, 
reduced risk, and gave him the assurance of water security.

The Challenge
Brisil Technologies extracts Green Silica from Rice Husk 
Ash- a byproduct of biofuel production that would 
otherwise be dumped, contributing to air, water, and 
soil pollution. By procuring this ash directly from rice 
mills and converting it into a valuable material, Brisil 
keeps waste out of the environment while producing a 
sustainable alternative to conventionally mined silica.
Brisil was operating at roughly 20–25% of its 
production capacity- a significant gap between what 
the facility could produce and what it was actually 
delivering each month.
How MIF & the Mentor Helped
The mentor conducted a Time Motion Study across all production 
stages to map workflows and surface bottlenecks. This was paired 
with end-to-end process documentation (raw material intake to 
final output) and a set of targeted manufacturing improvements. 
The mentor also introduced mistake-proofing techniques to reduce 
operational errors and shared ready-to-use formats for time 
motion studies and safety compliance.
The Result 
Through these combined interventions, 
Brisil moved from ~20–25% capacity 
utilisation to 100% - fully closing the 
gap between potential and actual output.

At Marico, the pursuit of energy conservation and GHG emission reduction is not 
a periodic initiative; it is embedded in the continuous rhythm of our operations 
and our long-term capital allocation decisions. Cognisant of the accelerating 
risks posed by climate change and the strategic imperative of securing energy 
resilience, we have institutionalized a robust, multi-layered carbon management 
framework that spans our entire manufacturing ecosystem and extends 
meaningfully into our value chain. Our approach is purposefully holistic; we 
simultaneously target energy demand reduction through operational efficiency, 
decarbonise our energy supply through renewable sourcing and generation, 
and deploy nature-based carbon sequestration as a supportive pathway. As we 
close in on our 2030 India net-zero target and our 2040 global commitment, the 
pace of action is unmistakably accelerating and FY26 results validate that our 
investments are delivering material outcomes.
Net Zero Ambition: Our 
Strategic Decarbonization 
Pathway
Aligned with our Vision 2030 ambitions 
and long-term climate commitments, 
our India operations are accelerating 
a structured transition towards deep 
decarbonisation. We have set a clear 
target to achieve a 93% reduction in 
Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse 
gas (GHG) emissions from our owned 
manufacturing facilities by 2030, against 
an FY13 baseline. The residual 7% of 
emissions will be neutralised through 
high-integrity carbon sequestration 
initiatives and certified offset mechanisms. 
As we advance along this trajectory, we 
have adopted a differentiated, forward-
looking decarbonisation framework that

Introduction 
Bureau Veritas (India) Private Limited (“Bureau Veritas”) has been commissioned by the management 
of Marico Limited (Corporate Identification Number (CIN): L15140MH1988PLC049208) (hereinafter 
referred to as “Marico” or “the Company”) to undertake an independent verification of the Company’s 
Carbon Neutrality Declaration for its Jalgaon and Perundurai Manufacturing Facilities for the reporting 
period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026. 
The verification has been conducted to assess the conformity of Marico’s carbon neutrality claim with 
the requirements of ISO 14068-1:2023, including the quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas 
(GHG) emissions, implementation of emission reduction measures, renewable energy transition, 
retirement of environmental attributes, and neutralization of residual emissions through verified carbon 
credits. 
Assurance Standards 
This verification engagement has been carried out in accordance with Bureau Veritas verification 
methodology, based on the principles and requirements of: 
• 
ISO 14064-3:2019 – Greenhouse gases — Specification with guidance for the verification and 
validation of greenhouse gas statements; 
• 
ISO 14068-1:2023 – Climate Change Management — Transition to Net Zero — Part 1: Carbon 
Neutrality; 
• 
Relevant principles of ISAE 3000 (Revised) – Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or 
Reviews of Historical Financial Information. 
The verification has been conducted at a Limited Assurance level. 
Reporting Criteria 
Marico has quantified and reported greenhouse gas emissions for the defined verification boundary 
using an operational control approach and established greenhouse gas accounting methodologies 
based on: 
• 
ISO 14064-1:2018 – Greenhouse Gases — Specification with guidance at the organizational 
level for quantification and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals; 
• 
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (Revised 
Edition); 
• 
Central Electricity Authority (CEA), Government of India, Grid Emission Factors for electricity-
related emissions; 
• 
IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) Global Warming Potentials (GWPs); 
• 
DEFRA Greenhouse Gas Reporting Conversion Factors; 
• 
Other internationally recognized emission factors and methodologies, where applicable. 
Marico is responsible for the preparation, presentation, and integrity of the greenhouse gas inventory, 
carbon neutrality claim, supporting calculations, renewable energy certificate retirement records, 
carbon credit retirement records, and all related information used in support of the carbon neutrality 
declaration.

At Marico, responsible sourcing is a strategic priority that extends our environmental 
ambitions beyond the physical boundaries of our owned operations into the 
complex, multi-tiered ecosystem of suppliers, co-manufacturers, logistics partners,

SAMYUT: Our Responsible Sourcing Architecture
Derived from the Sanskrit word meaning "coming together to achieve," SAMYUT reflects Marico's conviction that sustainability in 
the value chain is a shared pursuit, not a unilateral demand. The framework is aligned with key international conventions 
and standards, including the UN Sustainable Development Goals, SA 8000, the Universal Declaration of 
Human Rights, and the ILO’s Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work. The Sustainability 
Committee provides oversight for SAMYUT implementation and integration with procurement practices, ensuring decision-making 
alignment across our value chain. Purchasing practices towards suppliers are continuously reviewed to ensure alignment with the 
Code of Conduct and Responsible Sourcing Policy to avoid potential conflicts with ESG requirements. The framework covers all 
critical value chain partners; suppliers of raw and packaging materials, logistics and transportation partners, warehouse and depot 
associates, third-party manufacturers, and service providers and is built on three interconnected thrust areas:

Maturity-Based Transition Programme for Critical Supply Chain Partners
To drive continuous improvement and embed sustainability deeper into our supply chain, SAMYUT operates through a structured, 
three-level maturity pathway ensuring that supplier engagement progresses from awareness through evaluation to active co-creation 
of sustainability outcomes:
Level 1 – Educate
We initiate supplier engagement by communicating the Samyut requirements and creating 
awareness around responsible sourcing. Partners are expected to provide formal consent 
to adhere to the framework and complete a self-assessment of their ESG performance via a 
structured Level 1 questionnaire.
Level 2 – Evaluate
This phase introduces a comprehensive evaluation mechanism through external audits. 
The purpose is to validate supplier self-declarations, assess ESG-related risks, and monitor 
performance across key impact areas. Marico conducts regular performance reviews of 
critical suppliers under SAMYUT, with defined escalation procedures for non-compliance. 
The framework enables appropriate action where suppliers are unable to meet minimum 
ESG expectations within agreed timelines.
Level 3 – Evolve
At this stage, Marico partners with suppliers to implement joint improvement projects, offer 
technical expertise, and drive measurable improvement in sustainability KPIs. Partners are 
encouraged to publicly disclose performance metrics aligned with both Marico’s requirements 
and global sustainability standards. The framework allows for potential supplier support 
through remote or on-site assistance on corrective and improvement actions as circumstances 
permit. Marico provides targeted support to suppliers including on-site interventions, 
improvement action plans, and ongoing ESG capability building/trainings.

Marico's Pursuit of Traceability in Agricultural Sourcing
One of the most significant advancements in FY26 responsible sourcing has been the leap in assessing 
Traceability of agricultural raw material (by spends) upto location levels from 24% in FY25 to  
50% in FY26. This progress reflects the maturation of our strategic partnerships with certified farms, 
the deployment of technology-enabled traceability tools, and deepened engagement with our SAMYUT 
framework across agricultural supply chains. Achieving traceability upto location levels for cultivation 
and/or primary processing, is essential for climate risk assessment and mitigation planning in agricultural 
value chains, establishing credible deforestation-free sourcing claims, and the long-term integrity of our 
responsible sourcing program. 
Advancing Deforestation-Free Sourcing
Marico is committed to sourcing raw materials in a manner that actively safeguards natural ecosystems 
and biodiversity. Our deforestation-free sourcing commitments embedded in the SAMYUT framework and 
the Supplier Code for Responsible Sourcing in agri-based value chains are now backed by substantially 
stronger operational evidence. We are advancing end-to-end deforestation monitoring through satellite-
based land-use analytics, supplier declaration protocols aligned with emerging regulatory frameworks 
(including the EU Deforestation Regulation) and Accountability Framework initiative (AFi), and deepened 
partnership with suppliers from a biodiversity impact perspective. By strengthening traceability and 
engaging suppliers on sustainable land-use practices, we are building the supply chain integrity that long-
term environmental leadership demands.
Marico's commitment to nature-positive business is formalised through our Board-endorsed Biodiversity 
and No Deforestation Policy, which governs our approach across operations and value chains through 
six structured commitments. We conduct regular ecosystem and biodiversity assessments at all operational 
sites, applying the mitigation hierarchy avoid, minimise, restore, and offset to ensure no net deforestation 
across our footprint. Through our SAMYUT responsible sourcing framework, we actively engage suppliers 
to avoid activities near biodiversity-sensitive areas, while respecting the land rights and traditional 
knowledge of local communities in our sourcing geographies.

ECONOMIC SCENARIO
Global
At the start of the year under review, the global economy was 
expected to sustain a modest recovery. The macroeconomic 
outlook turned volatile in the recent months amidst the ongoing 
geopolitical developments, particularly in the Middle East, 
leading to some variability in global energy markets and 
operating environment.
Multilateral institutions have since revised their global growth 
outlook, citing the combined effects of elevated energy prices, 
tighter financial conditions, and softer global demand. Despite 
these headwinds, certain structural growth drivers remain intact, 
including ongoing investments in digital infrastructure and 
artificial intelligence.  Near-term global economic conditions 
are being influenced by geopolitical developments, energy 
market dynamics and fiscal conditions, alongside accelerating 
investments in digital and AI, collectively shaping demand 
patterns and cost structures.
India
India’s economic growth remained robust during the year, 
supported by strong domestic demand and sustained public 
investment. Growth was driven by resilient private consumption 
and investment momentum. Consumption benefitted from easing 
inflationary pressures and supportive fiscal measures, while 
investment was aided by declining interest rates and continued 
government capital expenditure. External demand remained 
relatively stable, with moderate export growth alongside higher 
imports reflecting strong domestic demand.
On the supply side, growth was led by both services and 
manufacturing sectors. Services activity expanded strongly, 
supported by financial services, real estate, professional services, 
trade, and hospitality. Manufacturing performance improved 
during the year, benefitting from strengthening domestic demand 
and easing input cost pressures. Agricultural output recorded 
moderate growth, supported by favourable weather conditions.
Inflationary pressures moderated over the course of the year, 
primarily driven by easing food prices and softer global 
commodity trends. Improved system liquidity and lower 
borrowing costs supported credit growth, reinforcing overall 
macroeconomic stability amid a volatile global backdrop.
Labour market conditions remained broadly stable with 
employment conditions improving in rural areas, while urban 
labour markets remained resilient.
Looking ahead, India’s growth outlook remains relatively resilient 
compared to global peers. Services and manufacturing sectors 
are expected to continue to drive economic activity, supported 
by domestic demand, policy initiatives, and improving business 
sentiment. Public investment is likely to remain a key anchor for 
infrastructure development and overall economic momentum, 
while agricultural performance will remain dependent on 
weather conditions.
According to the estimates from the Asian Development Bank, 
GDP growth is expected to moderate mildly in the near term 
before strengthening over the medium term, supported by 
consumption, investment, and ongoing structural reforms. 
Inflation is expected to remain within a manageable range, 
although subject to fluctuations due to food and energy prices 
and currency movements. Key downside risks to the outlook 
include heightened global uncertainties arising from geopolitical 
tensions, evolving trade policies, and volatility in energy prices. 
Bangladesh
Bangladesh’s economic growth moderated during the year with 
domestic demand remaining subdued amidst tight monetary and 
fiscal conditions, however, strong remittance inflows and relatively 
resilient industrial performance provided some support. The 
services sector experienced some moderation, while agricultural 
output was affected by unfavourable weather conditions.
Policy measures remained focused on maintaining macroeconomic 
stability, even as inflation continued to weigh on household 
purchasing power. Fiscal consolidation progressed, reducing the 
budget deficit and the monetary policy remained prudent in an 
effort to contain inflation and stabilize the external position. Strong 
growth in remittance inflows and recovering exports supported a 
shift towards a broadly balanced current account position. Foreign 
exchange reserves increased during the year to approximately 
four months of import cover. Greater exchange rate flexibility also 
helped enhance resilience.
According to estimates from the Asian Development Bank, 
economic growth is expected to recover gradually over the medium 
term, supported by improving domestic demand, a rebound 
in services activity, normalization of agricultural output, and 
improving investor sentiment. Consumption is expected to remain 
the primary growth driver, supported by sustained remittance 
inflows, while investment is likely to strengthen progressively as 
confidence improves and imports of capital goods recover. While 
near term volatility may persist due to geopolitical developments, 
strengthening external balances and continued policy initiatives 
are expected to support  the economy.
Vietnam
Vietnam’s economy remained strong during the year, with GDP 
growth accelerating year-on-year. Economic expansion was 
driven by robust manufacturing activity, a continued recovery 
in tourism supporting services growth, and steady domestic 
demand. Industrial activity benefitted from strong export-oriented 
manufacturing and construction, while consumer spending 
remained resilient. 
According to estimates from the Asian Development Bank, 
economic growth is expected to moderate slightly in the near 
term while remaining robust, supported by a significant scale‑up 
in public investment, continued accommodative monetary policy, 
and resilient domestic demand. Services activity is expected 
to remain strong, aided by sustained tourism recovery and 
expanding digital and financial services, while manufacturing 
is likely to benefit from stable global demand and supportive 
policy measures. The outlook remains subject to evolving 
external conditions, including changes in global trade dynamics, 
geopolitical developments and weather-related risks. 
Middle East and North Africa
Economic activity in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) 
region remained relatively resilient during the year, supported by 
both oil and non-oil sector and continued public investment. In 
the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, non‑hydrocarbon 
sectors, including manufacturing and services, continued to 
demonstrate resilience and remained key contributors to regional 
growth. Among oil‑importing economies, growth conditions 
improved, supported by easing import and foreign exchange 
restrictions, strengthening private demand, and favourable 
agricultural conditions. In Egypt, growth recovered during the 
year driven by private demand, alongside a gradual easing 
in inflation. Inflationary pressures across the region generally 
remained elevated, reflecting higher food and energy prices 
amid supply‑side disruptions. However, inflation was better 
contained in GCC economies. 
Towards the end of the year, geopolitical developments in 
West Asia led to volatility in energy prices and supply chains, 
however underlying demand drivers remained intact across both 
markets. According to the World Bank, growth in the Middle East 
and North Africa region is expected to moderate in the near 
term before improving gradually over the medium term as the 
geopolitical developments stabilise.
South Africa
South Africa’s economic activity improved during the year, 
supported primarily by resilient private consumption, alongside 
improving electricity availability and a gradual recovery in 
business confidence. Sectoral gains, including in agriculture 
and services, also provided some support to economic activity, 
although overall growth remained soft. Macroeconomic 
conditions remained broadly stable, underpinned by credible 
monetary policy and ongoing reform efforts. 
According to the International Monetary Fund and the World 
Bank, growth is expected to improve gradually over the medium 
term supported by sustained structural reforms particularly 
in energy and logistics and a progressive recovery in private 
investment, alongside continued strength in consumption.
FAST MOVING CONSUMER GOODS (FMCG) 
SECTOR IN INDIA
India’s consumption landscape continues to undergo a structural 
transformation, supported by rising disposable incomes, progress 
in tax and regulatory frameworks, rapid digital adoption, and a 
broadening aspiration base across both urban and rural markets. 
Private consumption remains a key driver of economic activity, 
aided by increasing formalisation and improving access to 
organised retail and digital platforms.
The retail ecosystem is evolving steadily, with a gradual 
shift in market share from traditional general trade formats 
towards modern trade, E‑Commerce, Quick Commerce, and 
direct‑to‑consumer channels. While general trade continues 
to account for a significant portion of overall retail, emerging 
channels are gaining traction, reflecting consumer preference for 
convenience, wider assortment, and faster fulfilment. Digital‑first 
and omnichannel models are increasingly influencing how FMCG 
products are discovered, purchased, and consumed.
Premiumisation and formalisation trends continue to strengthen 
across FMCG categories. Branded products are gaining share, 
supported by rising quality consciousness, increasing health 
awareness, and greater willingness among consumers to trade up 
within categories. New‑age and digital‑native brands are scaling-up 
rapidly by addressing differentiated consumer needs and niche 
segments through targeted innovation, data‑driven marketing, and 
direct consumer engagement.
Consumption growth in India is increasingly driven by distinct 
consumer cohorts. Affluent urban consumers account for a 
disproportionate share of branded and premium consumption. At 
the same time, increasing internet and smartphone penetration is 
helping bridge awareness and access gaps between urban and rural 
markets, accelerating the adoption of branded FMCG products.
Evolving consumption patterns are being shaped by several 
structural trends, including premiumisation, health and wellness 
orientation, greater influence of younger cohorts on household 
spending, rising participation of women in consumption decisions, 
increased demand for personalisation, and blurring of traditional 
category boundaries. Together, these factors are reshaping 
demand across FMCG categories and influencing innovation, 
pricing, and go‑to‑market strategies.
For FMCG companies, these shifts are expected to drive further 
opportunities across core and emerging categories, while 
also necessitating greater agility in portfolio management, 
channel strategy, supply chain, cost structures, and consumer 
engagement models.
